mainTopic: Famous הספדים and signs of mourning at the deaths of great חכמים
overview: The גמרא finishes the story of רבה בר הונא and רב המנונא, whose coffins were carried on camels. At a narrow bridge the camels stop, as if each rabbi is giving the other the honor of going first. An Arab who ranks one rabbi above the other is punished, and a child then gives a poetic הספד for the two rabbis. Next come famous הספדים: for רבינא, and the words בר קיפוק and בר אבין planned for him, which hurt רב אשי and brought a punishment on them. After a prayer by בר אבין at the river and a memory list of names, the גמרא tells of the הספדים for רבי חנין, רבי יוחנן and רבי זירא. Along the way it rules that a student mourns even his teacher for only one day. It then lists signs in nature that appeared when great sages died. At the end it introduces a new ברייתא, returning to the הלכות of mourning.

steps.title: The camels stop at the bridge
steps.stepSummary: When the funeral procession reaches a bridge, the camels carrying the two rabbis stand still.
steps.simpleTranslation: When they reached a bridge, the camels stood still.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the story of the two rabbis being carried for burial. It sets up a strange event: the camels stop and will not cross.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The bridge was narrow, so only one camel could cross at a time. The camels stopping is the puzzle that the next lines will explain.

phrases.english: When they reached a bridge,
the camels stood still.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי מְטוֹ אַגִּישְׁרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the burial story from earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The camels carrying the two rabbis stopped at the bridge.

steps.title: An Arab asks what is going on
steps.stepSummary: An Arab onlooker asks why the camels stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain Arab said to them: What is this?
steps.whatsHappening: A bystander asks about the strange sight. This question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question puts into words what any reader would ask: why would camels stop for no reason?

phrases.english: A certain Arab said to them:
What is this?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לְהוּ הַהוּא טַיָּיעָא מַאי הַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind the event in step 1.

steps.title: The rabbis are honoring each other
steps.stepSummary: The people explain that the two departed rabbis are each telling the other to go first.
steps.simpleTranslation: They told him: The rabbis are showing honor to one another. One says, 'Master, you go first,' and the other says, 'Master, you go first.'
steps.whatsHappening: The people answer the Arab. Even after death, the two rabbis are being polite, and each one wants the other to cross first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since only one could cross first, each rabbi was giving the honor to the other, so neither camel moved. This shows how deep their respect for each other was.

keyTerms.meaning: Master (a respectful way to address a rabbi)

phrases.english: They said to him:
These are rabbis who are showing honor to one another.
One master says: 'The master should go first,'
and the other master says: 'The master should go first.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן דְּקָא עָבְדִי יְקָרָא אַהֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the Arab's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The two rabbis are each giving the other the honor of crossing first.

steps.title: The Arab decides who goes first
steps.stepSummary: The Arab declares that רבה בר הונא should go first, and his camel crosses.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: By law, רבה בר הונא should go first. The camel of רבה בר הונא crossed.
steps.whatsHappening: The Arab decides between the two rabbis and says רבה בר הונא should go first. Right away, רבה בר הונא's camel crosses the bridge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By picking one rabbi over the other, the Arab put the second rabbi, רב המנונא, lower. The camel moving shows the deadlock was broken, but the next line shows this choice was disrespectful.

keyTerms.meaning: by law / it is right that

phrases.english: He said: It is the law
that רבה בר הונא should go first.
The camel of רבה בר הונא crossed,

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר דִּינָא הוּא דְּרַבָּה בַּר הוּנָא לֵיעוּל בְּרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The Arab steps in to settle the deadlock described in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Arab ruled that רבה בר הונא goes first, and his camel crossed.

steps.title: The Arab is punished
steps.stepSummary: The Arab's teeth fall out because he slighted the other rabbi.
steps.simpleTranslation: The molars and teeth of that Arab fell out.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the Arab's punishment: his teeth fall out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying one rabbi was greater, the Arab disrespected רב המנונא. The lesson is that one must be very careful with the honor of תלמידי חכמים, even after they die.
steps.whatToRemember: The two rabbis honored each other even in death, and the Arab who ranked one above the other was punished. The honor of a תלמיד חכם must be guarded carefully.

phrases.english: the molars and teeth of that Arab fell out.

steps.triggerLanguage: נְתוּר כַּכֵּיהּ וְשִׁנֵּיהּ דְּהָהוּא טַיָּיעָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the result of the Arab's choice in step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Disrespecting a תלמיד חכם, even by ranking him below another, brings punishment.

steps.title: A child's eulogy, part one: the rabbis came from בבל
steps.stepSummary: A child opens a הספד describing the two rabbis arriving from בבל and the great loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain child opened a eulogy for him: 'A shoot of ancient elders went up from בבל, and with him a book of wars. The pelican and the bittern have been doubled, to see the ruin and brokenness that came from שנער.'
steps.whatsHappening: Now a child gives a poetic הספד for the rabbis. This first part describes them coming up from בבל and calls their death a great destruction.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'A shoot of ancient elders' fits רבה בר הונא, who came from a great family. 'A book of wars' fits רב המנונא, a great Torah scholar. The pelican and bittern are birds of ruin, so the child is saying the destruction has doubled.

keyTerms.meaning: a shoot (descendant) of old, great people

phrases.english: A certain child opened a eulogy for him:
'A shoot of ancient elders has gone up from Babylonia,
and with him is a book of wars.
phrases.notes: The phrase comes from במדבר 21:14 and here means a person full of תורה.

phrases.english: The pelican and the bittern have been doubled,
phrases.notes: These birds live in ruined places (ישעיה 34:11), so they stand for destruction.

phrases.english: to see the ruin and brokenness that has come from Shinar.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ הַהוּא יָנוֹקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the bridge episode, the story moves on to the הספד for the two rabbis.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The child mourns the two great rabbis from בבל as a doubled destruction.

steps.title: A child's eulogy, part two: Heaven rejoices
steps.stepSummary: The child says ה׳ took these souls and rejoices over them like a new bride.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He became angry at His world and took souls from it, and He rejoices over them like a new bride. The One who rides the heavens is happy and glad when a pure and righteous soul comes to Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: The child finishes the הספד. Our world lost these souls, but ה׳ receives them with joy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הספד moves from sadness down here to joy above. ה׳ 'taking' souls is a sign of anger at the world, yet in Heaven a righteous soul is greeted like a new bride.

keyTerms.meaning: the One who rides the heavens (ה׳)

phrases.english: He became angry at His world
and seized souls from it,
and He rejoices over them like a new bride.
The One who rides the heavens is joyful and glad
when a pure and righteous soul comes to Him.'

steps.triggerLanguage: קָצַף עַל עוֹלָמוֹ וְחָמַס מִמֶּנּוּ נְפָשׁוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues and finishes the child's הספד from step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The death of the righteous is a loss for the world but a joy in Heaven.

steps.title: The eulogy for רבינא
steps.stepSummary: When רבינא died, a eulogizer compared him to a date palm and to someone who made nights like days.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבינא died, a certain eulogizer began: 'Date palms, bow your heads over the righteous one who was like a date palm. Let us make nights like days, over the one who made nights like days.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives another famous הספד, this time for רבינא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הספד uses two pictures. רבינא was like a tall date palm, so the palms should mourn him. He learned at night as if it were day, so we should cry at night as if it were day.

keyTerms.meaning: he passed away (literally, his soul rested)

phrases.english: When Ravina passed away,
a certain eulogizer opened a eulogy for him:
'Date palms, bow your heads
over the righteous one who was like a date palm.
phrases.notes: This picks up תהלים 92:13, 'a righteous man will flourish like a date palm.'

phrases.english: Let us make nights like days
phrases.notes: He means we should cry through the night.

phrases.english: over the one who made nights like days.'
phrases.notes: רבינא learned תורה at night as if it were daytime.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרָבִינָא פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ הַהוּא סַפְדָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story in a list of famous הספדים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבינא was mourned as a righteous date palm who learned through the night.

steps.title: רב אשי asks בר קיפוק what he will say
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks the famous eulogizer בר קיפוק what he says on 'that day'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to בר קיפוק: On that day, what do you say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a time before רבינא died. רב אשי asks the eulogizer בר קיפוק what he will say on the day רבינא dies. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'That day' means a day of death and mourning. The question gets us ready to hear בר קיפוק's opening words.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְבַר קִיפּוֹק:
phrases.english: Rav Ashi said to bar Kippok:
On that day, what do you say?
phrases.notes: 'That day' means the future day when רבינא would die. רב אשי asks this while רבינא is still alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אָשֵׁי לְבַר קִיפּוֹק הָהוּא יוֹמָא מַאי אָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to a conversation before רבינא's death about the eulogy planned for him.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What words בר קיפוק would open his הספד with.

steps.title: בר קיפוק's three pictures of loss
steps.stepSummary: בר קיפוק answers with three comparisons: if the great fall, what will the small do?
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: I say: 'If a flame fell on the cedars, what will the hyssop on the wall do? If the leviathan was pulled up with a hook, what will the little fish in the shallows do? If a hook fell into a flowing river, what will the puddle water do?'
steps.whatsHappening: בר קיפוק gives his opening lines. All three make the same point: if even the greatest person can die, how can small people feel safe?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each line pairs something great with something small: cedars and hyssop, the leviathan and little fish, a rushing river and puddles. If the great one could not escape, what hope do the small ones have?

keyTerms.meaning: hyssop growing on a wall (a tiny plant)
the leviathan, a giant sea creature
little fish of the shallow marsh

steps.whatToRemember: A good הספד reminds the living: if the great one has died, all the more must the rest of us think about our own lives.

phrases.english: He said to him: I say:
'If a flame has fallen upon the cedars,
what shall the hyssop of the wall do?
If the leviathan was pulled up with a hook,
what shall the fish of the shallows do?
If a hook has fallen into a flowing river,
what shall the water of the puddles do?'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אָמֵינָא אִם בַּאֲרָזִים נָפְלָה שַׁלְהֶבֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אשי's question from step 9.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Three comparisons showing that if the great have fallen, the small have even more reason to fear.

steps.title: בר אבין rejects the hook-and-flame wording
steps.stepSummary: בר אבין says it would be wrong to use words like 'hook' and 'flame' about צדיקים.
steps.simpleTranslation: בר אבין said to him: God forbid that I should say 'hook' and 'flame' about righteous people.
steps.whatsHappening: A second eulogizer, בר אבין, objects to the comparisons בר קיפוק just gave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 10, בר קיפוק compared the great people to cedars caught by a flame and to a לויתן pulled up by a hook. בר אבין says these pictures are not respectful enough for צדיקים. He is not arguing about the sadness of the loss. He is only objecting to the choice of words.

phrases.english: Bar Avin said to him:
God forbid that 'hook' and 'flame'
I should say about the righteous.

steps.triggerLanguage: חַס וְשָׁלוֹם דְּחַכָּה וְשַׁלְהֶבֶת בְּצַדִּיקֵי אָמֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the wording of בר קיפוק's answer in Step 10
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the images of hook and flame, not the idea of mourning
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Those images are not respectful when used for צדיקים

steps.title: What would you say instead?
steps.stepSummary: בר אבין is asked what eulogy he would give.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what would you say?
steps.whatsHappening: בר אבין is asked to offer his own version. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If you reject someone's wording, the natural follow-up is to ask for something better. The question moves the story from criticism to a positive suggestion.

phrases.english: And what would you say?
phrases.notes: רב אשי is the one asking, just as he questioned בר קיפוק in Step 9.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמַאי אָמְרַתְּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on בר אבין's objection

steps.title: Cry for the mourners, not for the one who left
steps.stepSummary: בר אבין's eulogy: weep for those left behind, because the departed soul is at rest.
steps.simpleTranslation: I would say: Cry for the mourners and not for what was lost, because what was lost has gone to rest, while we are left sighing.
steps.whatsHappening: בר אבין gives his gentler eulogy. It focuses on the pain of the living, not on the downfall of the צדיק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His version avoids any picture of the צדיק being caught or burned. The one who passed away is at peace, and the real loss belongs to the living. This is the respectful alternative to Step 10.

keyTerms.meaning: that which was lost (here, the departed soul)

phrases.english: I would say: Cry for the mourners
and not for the lost one, for it has gone to rest
phrases.notes: The 'lost one' means the soul of the person who died.

phrases.english: while we are left to sighing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמֵינָא: בְּכוּ לָאֲבֵלִים וְלֹא לָאֲבֵידָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 12
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A eulogy that mourns for the living, since the departed soul is at rest

steps.title: The eulogizers are punished and cannot attend
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי was upset with them, their feet became bent, and neither came to eulogize רבינא.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was upset with them, and their feet turned over. On that day, they did not come to eulogize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The story continues: the two eulogizers are punished, and as a result they miss רבינא's actual הספד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Their eulogies compared רבינא to cedars and a לויתן, and the other חכמים, including רב אשי, to tiny hyssop and little fish. רב אשי was hurt by this, and because of his anger their feet became twisted. So when רבינא actually died, neither of them could come to eulogize him.

phrases.english: He was upset with them,
phrases.notes: The one who was upset is רב אשי, who had been asking them about their eulogies.

phrases.english: and their feet turned over.
On that day, they did not come to eulogize him.
phrases.notes: 'That day' means the day רבינא actually died.

steps.triggerLanguage: חֲלַשׁ דַּעְתֵּיהּ עֲלַיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells what happened as a result of the eulogy discussion
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The eulogizers were punished and missed רבינא's real funeral

steps.title: רב אשי's saying about חליצה
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי described the episode with a picture: neither of them can do חליצה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רב אשי meant: Neither בר קיפוק can do חליצה, nor can בר אבין do חליצה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects a known saying of רב אשי to this story and explains what it was about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חליצה requires removing a shoe from the foot in the normal way. With their feet twisted, these two could not do it properly. רב אשי's saying is a word-picture of their punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: and this is what he meant when he said

phrases.english: And this is what Rav Ashi said:
Neither can bar Kippok do chalitza,
phrases.notes: For חליצה the shoe has to come off the foot properly, which bent feet can't do.

phrases.english: nor can bar Avin do chalitza.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a saying of רב אשי using the story of Step 14
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב אשי's saying about חליצה refers to the twisted feet of the two eulogizers
steps.whatToRemember: The two eulogizers spoke about רבינא in a way that hurt רב אשי. Their feet became bent, so they missed the real הספד, and רב אשי said neither could do חליצה.

steps.title: רבא asks בר אבין to speak at the river
steps.stepSummary: When רבא came to the Tigris, he asked בר אבין to say something.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבא came to the Tigris, he said to בר אבין: Get up and say something.
steps.whatsHappening: A new short story about בר אבין begins. This line sets up the prayer he says in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Crossing a big river was dangerous, so רבא asks the skilled speaker בר אבין to pray. The content comes next.

phrases.english: Rava, when he came to the Tigris,
said to bar Avin:
Get up and say something.
phrases.notes: He means a prayer for their safety on the water.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא, כִּי הֲוָה אֲתָא לְדִגְלַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story about the same speaker, בר אבין
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבא asks בר אבין to pray at the river

steps.title: בר אבין's prayer on the water
steps.stepSummary: בר אבין prays: most of the third has come into the water, so remember and have mercy, and do not punish us with water.
steps.simpleTranslation: He stood and said: Most of the third has come into the water, remember and have mercy. We strayed from You like a woman from her husband, but do not abandon us like the sign of the bitter water.
steps.whatsHappening: בר אבין gives a short poetic prayer asking ה׳ to protect them on the river.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Most of the third' is a poetic name for the Jewish people, suggesting that רבא is worth most of כלל ישראל. He admits that the people have strayed like an unfaithful wife. He asks that they not be punished with water, the way a סוטה is tested with the bitter water.

keyTerms.meaning: most of the third, a poetic name for the Jewish people

phrases.english: He stood and said:
Most of the third has come into the water,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 19:24. 'The third' is the Jewish people, so רבא counts as most of them.

phrases.english: remember and have mercy.
We strayed from You like a woman from her husband,
do not abandon us like the sign of the bitter water.
phrases.notes: This is the water used to test a סוטה. He is asking: don't punish us through water.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָאֵי וְאָמַר: בָּאוּ רוֹב שְׁלִישִׁית בְּמַיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the prayer that רבא requested in Step 16
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A prayer asking for mercy and protection on the water

steps.title: A memory aid for the next stories
steps.stepSummary: A list of names serves as a סימן to remember the order of the stories that follow.
steps.simpleTranslation: חנין, יוחנן, זירא, אבא, יעקב, יוסי, שמואל, חייא, מנחם: this is a memory aid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a list of names to help us remember the next stories. It is setting up what comes next and is not a teaching on its own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each name points to a story that will come next about eulogies for great people. The list itself says nothing new. It only keeps the order of the stories straight.
steps.confusionAlert: This list is not a statement or a ruling. It is only a memory device for the stories that follow.

phrases.english: (Chanin, Yochanan, Zeira, Abba,
phrases.notes: This is a memory list of names, not part of the discussion itself. Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.aramaic: יַעֲקֹב, יוֹסֵי, שְׁמוּאֵל, חִיָּיא, מְנַחֵם סִימָן).
phrases.english: Yaakov, Yosei, Shmuel, Chiyya, Menachem: a memory aid).

steps.triggerLanguage: חָנִין, יוֹחָנָן, זֵירָא, אַבָּא, יַעֲקֹב, יוֹסֵי, שְׁמוּאֵל, חִיָּיא, מְנַחֵם סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Transition to a new series of eulogy stories
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A memory aid listing the names in the stories that follow

steps.title: רבי חנין dies on the day his son is born
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנין, son-in-law of the נשיא's family, had no children. He prayed and was granted a son, but he died on the very day the son was born.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חנין married into the family of the נשיא. He had no children, so he prayed and was given a child. On the day the child was born, רבי חנין died.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story, the first in the list of names from the סימן. It sets the scene for the eulogy that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The details pile up the sadness: years without children, a prayer that was answered, and then death on the day of the birth. This background is what makes the eulogizer's words in the next step so painful.

keyTerms.meaning: The household of the נשיא (head of the Jewish community)
He passed away (literally, his soul rested)

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חָנִין, חַתְנֵיהּ דְּבֵי נְשִׂיאָה הֲוָה.
phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥanin was a son-in-law of the house of the Nasi.
He did not have children.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets. The meaning stays the same either way.

phrases.english: He prayed for mercy, and then he had them.
On that day when he had a child,
he passed away.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חָנִין, חַתְנֵיהּ דְּבֵי נְשִׂיאָה הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the first of the stories listed in the סימן of step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Narrative: רבי חנין died on the day his prayed-for son was born.

steps.title: The eulogy for רבי חנין and naming his son
steps.stepSummary: A eulogizer mourns that joy and sorrow came together. The baby was named חנן after his father.
steps.simpleTranslation: A eulogizer began: Happiness turned into sorrow, joy and grief became stuck together. At the moment of his happiness he sighed his last breath; at the moment he was graced with a child, the one who was graced was lost. They named the baby חנן after his father.
steps.whatsHappening: The eulogizer puts the tragedy into short poetic lines. Then the גמרא says the baby was named after his father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The last line is a play on רבי חנין's name, which comes from חן, grace. He was 'graced' with a son, yet he himself was lost. Naming the baby חנן keeps the father's name alive.

keyTerms.meaning: A eulogizer, someone who gives a הספד
After his name, named for him

phrases.english: A certain eulogizer opened his eulogy for him:
Happiness has turned into sorrow;
joy and grief have become joined together.
At the time of his happiness, he sighed;
at the time he was graced, his gracious one was lost.
phrases.notes: This is a play on the name חנין. He was 'graced' with a son, but he himself, the חנין, was lost.

phrases.english: They named the child Ḥanan after him.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ הַהוּא סַפְדָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the eulogy for the death described in step 19 and closes the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The eulogy describes joy turned into grief; the son is named for his father.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן's death is like the sun setting at noon
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בן אלעזר eulogizes רבי יוחנן: today is as hard for ישראל as the day the sun set at noon, quoting a פסוק in עמוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן died, רבי יצחק בן אלעזר began: Today is as hard for ישראל as the day the sun went down at noon, as it says, 'On that day I will bring the sun down at noon.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new story: the eulogy for רבי יוחנן. The eulogizer compares his death to the sun setting in the middle of the day, and backs this up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sun setting at noon means light ending far too early and without warning. The eulogizer uses a פסוק so the comparison has a source; the next step explains which day that פסוק is about.

keyTerms.meaning: Noon, the middle of the day
As it is written (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: When Rabbi Yoḥanan passed away,

phrases.aramaic: פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ רַבִּי יִצְחָק בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar opened his eulogy for him:
Today is as difficult for Israel
as the day the sun set at noon,
as it is written: "And it shall come to pass on that day
that I will cause the sun to set at noon."
phrases.notes: עמוס 8:9

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ רַבִּי יִצְחָק בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next story in the סימן list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן's death is compared to the sun setting at noon, based on the פסוק in עמוס.

steps.title: The פסוק refers to the day of King יאשיהו
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן himself had taught that this פסוק refers to the day King יאשיהו died.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: That day is the day of יאשיהו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the פסוק just quoted, using a teaching of רבי יוחנן himself. The 'sun setting at noon' was the death of King יאשיהו.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So the פסוק describes the death of a great צדיק as the sun going down. That is why it fits as a eulogy for רבי יוחנן, the great leader of his generation. Fittingly, it is his own teaching that is used about him.

keyTerms.meaning: King Yoshiyahu, a righteous king of יהודה

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: זֶה יוֹמוֹ שֶׁל יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ.
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: This is the day of Josiah.
phrases.notes: He means the day King יאשיהו was killed in battle.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: זֶה יוֹמוֹ שֶׁל יֹאשִׁיָּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the פסוק quoted in step 21, showing why it fits a great צדיק's death.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'sun setting at noon' in עמוס refers to the death of יאשיהו.

steps.title: רבי אמי mourns רבי יוחנן for seven and thirty days
steps.stepSummary: When רבי יוחנן died, his student רבי אמי sat in mourning for שבעה and שלושים, like a close relative.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי יוחנן died, רבי אמי sat in mourning for seven days and thirty days.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רבי אמי mourned his teacher רבי יוחנן. This sets up the next step, which asks whether this is the הלכה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבעה and שלושים are normally kept only for close relatives. רבי אמי kept them for his teacher, which raises a question: must every student do this?

keyTerms.meaning: The first seven days of mourning

phrases.english: When Rabbi Yoḥanan passed away,
Rabbi Ami sat in mourning for seven and thirty days.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, יָתֵיב רַבִּי אַמֵּי שִׁבְעָה וּשְׁלֹשִׁים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second story about רבי יוחנן's death, now about mourning practice rather than eulogy.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אמי kept שבעה and שלושים for his teacher רבי יוחנן.

steps.title: רבי אמי's mourning was a personal choice
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא says רבי אמי did this on his own; it is not the הלכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא son of רבי חייא בר אבא said: What רבי אמי did, he did for himself.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא steps in so no one learns the wrong הלכה from רבי אמי's story. His mourning was an extra, personal choice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A story about a great sage could easily be taken as the rule. רבי אבא blocks that: רבי אמי went beyond what is required. The next step gives the source for this.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not learn from רבי אמי's story that one must keep שבעה and שלושים for a teacher. The גמרא says clearly that this was his own personal practice.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Abba, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, said:
What Rabbi Ami did,
he did for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אַמֵּי דַּעֲבַד — לְגַרְמֵיהּ הוּא דַּעֲבַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the story of step 23 so it is not taken as binding halacha.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי אמי's שבעה and שלושים for his teacher was a personal stringency, not the הלכה.

steps.title: One mourns even one's teacher for only one day
steps.stepSummary: Proof from רבי יוחנן himself: even for the teacher who taught a person wisdom, one sits in mourning for only one day.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: Even for his teacher who taught him wisdom, a person sits in mourning for him only one day.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא brings the source for his claim. It is a teaching of רבי יוחנן, the very teacher רבי אמי was mourning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה is that a student mourns his teacher for one day only. So רבי אמי's seven and thirty days went far beyond the rule. The source is quoted through רבי אבא's own father, רבי חייא בר אבא.

keyTerms.meaning: For so, because this is how (introduces a source)
His teacher who taught him wisdom (Torah)

steps.whatToRemember: A student mourns even his main Torah teacher for only one day. רבי אמי's longer mourning for רבי יוחנן was his own personal choice.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the הלכה for mourning a teacher and shows that a sage's personal practice is not automatically the rule for everyone.

phrases.aramaic: דְּהָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: For so said Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, that Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Even for his teacher who taught him wisdom,

phrases.aramaic: אֵינוֹ יוֹשֵׁב עָלָיו אֶלָּא יוֹם אֶחָד.
phrases.english: one sits in mourning over him for only one day.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהָכִי אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source that backs up רבי אבא's claim in step 24.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי אמי's mourning of seven and thirty days was a personal practice and not required.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יוחנן's ruling, through רבי חייא בר אבא, that even one's main teacher is mourned for only one day.

steps.title: The eulogy for רבי זירא: born in בבל, raised in ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: A eulogizer mourns רבי זירא: born in בבל, raised in ארץ ישראל, and now טבריה mourns the loss of its treasured vessel.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי זירא died, a eulogizer began: The land of שנער conceived and gave birth; the land of beauty raised its darling. Woe to her, said רקת, for she has lost her precious vessel.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story: the eulogy for רבי זירא. It uses poetic names for places to tell his life story and the loss felt by his city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא was born in בבל (called ארץ שנער) and moved to ארץ ישראל (called ארץ צבי), where he grew great. רקת is a poetic name for טבריה, the city that lost him.

keyTerms.meaning: The land of Shinar, meaning בבל
The land of beauty, meaning ארץ ישראל
Rakkath, a poetic name for טבריה

phrases.english: When Rabbi Zeira passed away,
a certain eulogizer opened his eulogy for him:
The land of Shinar conceived and gave birth,
phrases.notes: שנער is בבל, where רבי זירא was born.

phrases.english: the land of beauty raised her darling.
phrases.notes: ארץ צבי is ארץ ישראל, where he moved and grew up in Torah.

phrases.english: Woe to her, said Rakkath,
phrases.notes: רקת is another name for טבריה, the city where he lived.

phrases.english: for she has lost her precious vessel.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא, פְּתַח עֲלֵיהּ הַהוּא סַפְדָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next eulogy story in the series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Eulogy for רבי זירא: born in בבל, raised in ארץ ישראל, and mourned by טבריה.

steps.title: Signs at the deaths of the sages of ארץ ישראל
steps.stepSummary: When the sages of ארץ ישראל died, nature reacted: pillars wept water, gutters ran with blood, stars appeared by day, trees were uprooted, fiery stones fell, and statues became smooth.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי אבהו died, the pillars of קיסרי ran with water. When רבי יוסי died, the gutters of ציפורי flowed with blood. When רבי יעקב died, the stars were seen during the day. When רבי אסי died, all the trees were uprooted. When רבי חייא died, fiery stones fell from the sky. When רבי מנחם son of רבי יוסי died, the statues became smooth, as if smoothed with a plasterer's tool.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues the theme of mourning great sages. It lists amazing things that happened in nature when certain sages of ארץ ישראל died.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list shows that the death of a צדיק is a loss for the whole world, not only for his students and family. Each sign fits the man or his city. The pillars of his own city 'cry' for רבי אבהו, and the gutters of his own city run with blood for רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: His soul rested: a respectful way of saying 'he passed away'
Caesarea, the city of רבי אבהו
Tzippori, the city of רבי יוסי

steps.confusionAlert: From the second sage on, the words 'כי נח נפשיה' (when he passed away) are not repeated. Every short 'ד...' line means 'when so-and-so passed away.'

phrases.english: When Rabbi Abbahu passed away,
the pillars of Caesarea ran with water.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, שְׁפַעוּ מַרְזְבֵי דְצִיפּוֹרִי דְּמָא.
phrases.english: When Rabbi Yosei passed away, the gutters of Tzippori flowed with blood.
When Rabbi Ya'akov passed away, the stars were visible during the day.
When Rabbi Asi passed away, all the trees were uprooted.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא, נְחִיתוּ כֵּיפֵי דְנוּרָא מֵרְקִיעָא.
phrases.english: When Rabbi Ḥiyya passed away, fiery stones fell from the sky.
When Rabbi Menaḥem, son of Rabbi Yosei, passed away,
the statues became smooth, as if smoothed with a plasterer's trowel.
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't. It means a plasterer's smoothing tool, so the statues' faces were wiped smooth.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of mourning great sages that began with the eulogy for רבי זירא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When great sages of ארץ ישראל died, nature itself showed signs of mourning.

steps.title: Signs at the deaths of more sages, mostly of בבל
steps.stepSummary: The list continues: statues were damaged, thieves dug tunnels in נהרדעא, hail fell, the bridges of the פרת and the דגלת collapsed, and palm trees became loaded with thorns.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי תנחום בר חייא died, all the king's statues were broken. When רבי אלישיב died, seventy tunnels were dug in נהרדעא. When רב המנונא died, hailstones fell from the sky. When רבה and רב יוסף died, the bridges of the פרת collapsed so their tops touched each other. When אביי and רבא died, the bridges of the דגלת did the same. When רבי משרשיא died, the palm trees became loaded with thorns.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its list of signs in nature, now mostly about sages who lived in בבל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some signs show what the sage had been protecting while he was alive. Once רבי אלישיב was gone, thieves could dig into houses in his town. The pairs רבה and רב יוסף, and אביי and רבא, get one shared sign, because they are famous pairs who learned together.

keyTerms.meaning: Statues, especially statues of the king
A tunnel dug by thieves to break into a house
Neharde'a, a major Jewish town in בבל
The Euphrates and the Tigris rivers

steps.whatToRemember: The death of a great Torah scholar is a loss for the whole world. The גמרא shows this through the signs nature gave when each sage died.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי תַּנְחוּם בַּר חִיָּיא, אִיתְקַצַּצוּ כֹּל אַנְדְּרָטַיָּא.
phrases.english: When Rabbi Tanḥum bar Ḥiyya passed away, every statue was mutilated.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבִּי אֶלְיָשִׁיב, אִיחֲתַרוּ שִׁבְעִין מַחְתַּרְתָּא בִּנְהַרְדְּעָא.
phrases.english: When Rabbi Elyashiv passed away, seventy tunnels were dug in Neharde'a.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַב הַמְנוּנָא, נְחִיתוּ כֵּיפֵי דְבַרְדָּא מֵרְקִיעָא.
phrases.english: When Rav Hamnuna passed away, hailstones fell from the sky.

phrases.aramaic: דְּרַבָּה וְרַב יוֹסֵף, נְשׁוּק כֵּיפֵי דִפְרָת אַהֲדָדֵי.
phrases.english: When Rabba and Rav Yosef passed away, the bridges of the Euphrates touched each other.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאַבָּיֵי וְרָבָא, נְשׁוּק כֵּיפֵי דְּדִגְלַת אַהֲדָדֵי.
phrases.english: When Abaye and Rava passed away, the bridges of the Tigris touched each other.
When Rabbi Mesharshiyya passed away,
the palm trees became laden with thorns.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּרַבִּי תַּנְחוּם בַּר חִיָּיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same list of signs in nature, moving on to more sages.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Nature showed signs of mourning at the deaths of more great sages, ending the list with רבי משרשיא.

steps.title: Introducing a new ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new ברייתא with the formula 'תנו רבנן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught in a ברייתא:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is only a setup. The גמרא is about to quote a ברייתא and is getting the next move ready.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the stories about the sages' deaths finished, the גמרא goes back to discussing the הלכות of mourning. 'תנו רבנן' tells us that the next source is a ברייתא, a teaching of the תנאים that is not in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: A teaching of the תנאים that was not included in the משנה

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the story section and turns back to the halachic discussion of mourning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup line: a ברייתא is about to be quoted.
